Type a place — Kyoto, Lagos, a village you grew up near — and get live conditions, the next 24 hours and a seven-day outlook in seconds.

Skyline is a personal demo project, not client work. It is hand-built in plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and every number it shows is live data pulled straight from the free Open-Meteo public API — nothing here is simulated or pre-recorded.

      Cities this week

      Four skies worth knowing about

      A standing selection of climates rather than a news feed: what each place is made of geographically, and when its weather is at its most likeable. No forecasts here — those live upstairs.

      Subpolar oceanic · Cfc

      Reykjavík

      Iceland · on Faxaflói bay, near the Arctic Circle

      One of the northernmost capital regions on Earth, and far milder than its latitude promises because the North Atlantic Drift keeps arriving with warm water. Maritime air masses collide here routinely, which is why local weather turns over several times in a day. Winter brings very short days and aurora season; summer brings light that hardly ends.

      When to go Late June to early August for continuous daylight — February to March if the aurora is the point.

      Search “Reykjavík” above for live conditions
      Humid subtropical · Cfa

      Tokyo

      Japan · the Kantō Plain, facing the bay

      A vast plain-city with the ocean a short train ride from the centre and four genuinely separate seasons. Winters tend to be dry and bright under cold north-west winds, spring is mild and blossom-famed, early summer arrives with the rainy season, and late summer turns hot, humid and typhoon-prone.

      When to go Late March to early April for the blossom, or October to November for the clearest, driest air.

      Search “Tokyo” above for live conditions
      Hot semi-arid · BSh

      Marrakesh

      Morocco · inland plain below the High Atlas

      Set on a high plain at the foot of the snow-capped High Atlas, so the forecast reads two landscapes at once: baked, rain-scarce city below, alpine ridge above. Summer heat is severe and rain is a rarity, while winter days stay mild in the sun and cool off sharply once it sets.

      When to go March to May, or October and November, when the medina is comfortably walkable by day.

      Search “Marrakesh” above for live conditions
      Tropical rainforest · Af

      Singapore

      Singapore · just off the equator, on the Malacca Strait

      A degree or so from the equator, so day length barely shifts across the year and the temperature holds in a narrow band — rain, not heat, is what makes the weather here. The monsoons trade wet seasons back and forth across the strait, and convective thunderstorms build most afternoons.

      When to go February to early April, the driest stretch of the year, still humid and still green.

      Search “Singapore” above for live conditions

The artwork on these four cards is hand-drawn illustration, not photography. For an actual reading, use the dashboard: anything with a live dot comes from Open-Meteo at request time.

      How the data works

      Two public endpoints, called straight from your browser

      Skyline has no server of its own. It is a static page that makes two HTTP requests, in this order, and renders exactly what comes back.

      1. Geocode the place you typed

        Your search text goes to Open-Meteo’s geocoding endpoint, which answers with up to five matches — each carrying a name, region, country and, crucially, a latitude and longitude. That is what fills the suggestion list under the search box.

        Step 1 · geocodinghttps://geocoding-api.open-meteo.com/v1/search?name=..&count=5&language=en&format=json

      2. Ask for the forecast at those coordinates

        Choosing a match fires a second request for that exact point: current temperature, humidity, apparent temperature, weather code and wind; hourly temperature and precipitation probability for the 24-hour chart; and daily maxima, minima, weather code, sunrise and sunset for seven days.

        Step 2 · forecasthttps://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=..&longitude=..&current=..&hourly=..&daily=..&timezone=auto&forecast_days=7

      3. Render it, honestly

        With timezone=auto the API replies in the city’s own local time, so the clock, sunrise and sunset all belong to the place you searched — not to wherever you happen to be. Night-time swaps the clear-sky icon for a moon. If you search again mid-flight, the outstanding request is cancelled rather than allowed to land out of order.

      No key. No account. No backend.

      There is no API key hidden in this page, no sign-in, and no proxy server of mine sitting between you and the data. The requests leave your browser for Open-Meteo directly.

      The only thing stored is your last chosen city and unit, in this browser’s localStorage, so the dashboard reopens where you left it. Location access is used only if you press the crosshair, and those coordinates never go anywhere except the forecast request.

      Open-Meteo publishes non-commercial use of its API for free, which is the whole reason a personal project like this can show real numbers at all. Data by Open-Meteo.com.

      Reading the forecast

      What the fields on screen actually mean

      Weather numbers are easy to read and easy to misread. A short glossary for the labels Skyline shows.

      Apparent temperature — “feels like”
      The temperature the air seems to be, once humidity, wind and sunlight are folded in, rather than the dry-bulb air temperature on its own. Wind strips away the warm layer your body holds close, so moving air reads colder; humid air blocks evaporation from skin, so it reads warmer. It is an index of human heat exchange, not a separate physical measurement of the atmosphere.
      Weather code
      A number from the WMO code 4677 table — the international shorthand weather services exchange. It is a category, not a count of drops: one code covers a light drizzle and a moderate one. Open-Meteo returns the code; Skyline maps it to a phrase and a hand-drawn icon.
      • 0 — clear sky
      • 1–3 — mainly clear to overcast
      • 45, 48 — fog and rime fog
      • 51–57 — drizzle, incl. freezing
      • 61–67 — rain, incl. freezing
      • 71–77 — snowfall and grains
      • 80–82 — rain showers
      • 85, 86 — snow showers
      • 95–99 — thunderstorm, with hail
      Daily minimum and maximum
      The lowest and highest air temperature expected across that calendar day in the city’s own timezone — not in the twenty-four hours from now. That distinction matters when you are reading a forecast for a place on the other side of you: the low may still be hours away in your terms.
      Rain chance
      Shown as bars behind the 24-hour line and as a percentage per day. It is the probability of at least a wetting amount falling — commonly taken as 0.2 mm or more — not a statement of how heavy it will be. A high chance can still mean a brief shower; a low one is not a guarantee of dry.
      Sunrise, sunset and the local clock
      Computed from the location and timezone of the city you searched. The header clock ticks in that zone, so it can legitimately disagree with your own watch, and the day-one row in the 7-day strip uses it as “today”.

      Where the limits are. Forecast skill falls away with lead time, so the last days of the strip are a tendency rather than a promise, and a city-sized error in the geocoding choice can put you somewhere unexpected — the suggestion list shows the region and country for that reason. This is also a personal demo: if a request fails, there is no cache or second provider to fall back on, so the page says so plainly and offers Retry instead of showing you a stale number.
